caption:
Is laser safe for darker skin?
Honestly, "safe" is an unfinished sentence.

A laser is aimed at one thing - a vessel, a spot, water. Melanin in the skin above absorbs part of that energy on the way through. More melanin means more heat arriving where nobody aimed it. This is not about how skin looks. It is about what absorbs light.

Reviews of energy-based devices describe a higher risk of pigmentation and scarring in higher Fitzpatrick types, and describe which approaches spare melanin better. A narrative review is not a rate, so it cannot tell you your own odds. What it tells you is that "this device is safe" needs "for which skin" added to the end of it.

Three questions before the first pass: which skin type am I in your assessment, is this device chosen for that type, and what do we do if pigment appears afterwards.

One thing worth knowing in advance: after some pigment treatments the spots look darker for a week or two before they clear. That part is expected. Pigment that keeps darkening after a low-energy session is a different thing, and it is worth going back in.

General education only.

#SkinOfColour #LaserSafety #KoreanAesthetics #MedicalAesthetics #BetterDecisions
first_comment: The third question is the one that separates clinics. Not because pigment is a failure - it is a known possibility - but because having a plan for it means someone has met it before.
